rv.q: That clarity also defines Keith Surney’s directorial debut, a bold and fearless entry that takes genuine risks—some raw, some revelatory— announcing a director unafraid to challenge both text and audience.
The principals involved make this excellent production gripping.

Dutchman (the play's title evokes both the Dutch slave ships of the Middle Passage and the recursive and inescapable fate of the legendary Flying Dutchman ghost ship) is raw, confrontational, poetic, and sometimes maddening, but its pull for audiences and other playwrights remains palpable, as Surney's staging demonstrates.
Surney does a skillful job in his directorial debut; he and the other actors keep the pace of this short, thrilling drama.
In any era, on any stage, this is an ugly play.
While the questions that Baraka raises are interesting, the presentation is chaotic and confusing.

cn.t: Baraka's incendiary 1964 allegory divides critics: some praise its political urgency and strong performances, while others question whether its confrontational, dated approach merits revival in 2025.
